title: Assessing Vasectomy-Related Information on YouTube: An Analysis of the Quality, Understandability, and Actionability of Information
screen_reason: Content analysis of 78 YouTube videos returned for the keyword “vasectomy”, with an explicit falsity code judged against urological guidelines: false statements regarding vasectomy were made in 14 (17.9%) videos. A share of items coded false with a stated denominator, so CONTENT applies. The DISCERN and PEMAT-A/V scoring in the same paper is QUALITY and is recorded separately.

estimates.country: Not stated for the videos; search run in the United States and appraised against American and Canadian urological guidelines
estimates.measure_type: % of vasectomy-related YouTube videos containing false statements about vasectomy
estimates.value_raw: False statements regarding vasectomy were made in 14 (17.9%) videos [the Results text instead reads: “False statements were made by both physicians and vloggers (video bloggers) in 13 (17%) videos”]
estimates.denominator: 78 videos retained from the first 100 YouTube search results for “vasectomy” (exclusions: duplicates, videos not relevant to vasectomy, videos where vasectomy was ancillary to another condition or intervention); the videos had 16,900,379 total views
estimates.definition: Video coded as containing a false statement about vasectomy, “mostly characterized by an underscoring of risks associated with vasectomy, claim of immediate effect without mentioning the post-vasectomy ineffective period, and falsely low vasectomy reversal rates”, judged against American Urological Association and Canadian Urological Association vasectomy guidelines and a systematic review of vasectomy safety and effectiveness
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; falsity is operationalised through the clinical variables drawn from the AUA and CUA vasectomy guidelines and Schwingl & Guess (2000), with the examples given being understated risks, claimed immediate effect ignoring the post-vasectomy ineffective period, and falsely low reversal rates.
estimates.source_quote: False statements regarding vasectomy were made in 14 (17.9%) videos.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract; the same finding appears in Results, “Video Selection and Characteristics”, as 13 (17%)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent evaluators, a medical student (primary coder, 100% of videos, whose data were used for analysis) and a urology resident who recoded a randomly selected 40%; inter-rater reliability by percent absolute agreement was 91% for the study-specific characteristics (which include the false-statement variable), 85% for PEMAT-A/V and 61% for DISCERN
estimates.moderator_quote: A YouTube search with the keyword “vasectomy” was conducted on May 18, 2020. The video title and URL of the first one hundred search results were recorded as this number encapsulates the most suggested videos while accounting for limited resources available for screening.
estimates.notes: NUMBER DISCREPANCY the adjudicator must see: the abstract says 14 (17.9%), the Results text says 13 (17%). 14/78 = 17.9% is internally consistent; 13/78 = 16.7%, so the Results pair is not. The abstract figure is used and both are recorded verbatim in value_raw. Either way the value sits between 16.7% and 17.9%. Rank-truncated sample (first 100 search results), hence denom_selection=curated. Country coded United States because the search was run from a US institution and the ground truth is AUA/CUA guidance; the paper never states a country restriction on the videos, so an adjudicator applying the “unspecified → Global” rule literally would code Global instead.

estimates.country: Not stated for the videos; search run in the United States and appraised against American and Canadian urological guidelines
estimates.measure_type: % of vasectomy-related YouTube videos scoring in the “fair” band of the DISCERN instrument (all remaining videos scored “poor” or worse; none scored good or excellent)
estimates.value_raw: Nine videos (11.5%) received scores in the “fair” range, while the remaining videos were scored as “poor”
estimates.denominator: 78 videos retained from the first 100 YouTube search results for “vasectomy”
estimates.definition: Video's summed DISCERN score (16 items, each 1–5, maximum 80) fell in the “fair” interpretation band; the median score across all videos was 28 (IQR 22–33), mean 28.7 (SD 7.3), range 15 to 46
estimates.misinfo_def: Not applicable; DISCERN measures the reliability and completeness of consumer treatment information, not veracity.
estimates.source_quote: Nine videos (11.5%) received scores in the “fair” range, while the remaining videos were scored as “poor”
estimates.page_loc: Results, “Quality, Understandability, and Actionability Results — DISCERN”; the same paragraph reports the median DISCERN score of 28 (IQR 22–33), mean 28.7 (±7.3), range 15 to 46
estimates.ground_truth_detail: DISCERN scored by a medical student for all videos, with a urology resident recoding a random 40%; inter-rater reliability was only 61% absolute agreement, so a third reviewer rescored all videos and reliability stayed at 60%, though mean scores fell within two points across raters. The authors list DISCERN's subjectivity and its lack of validation for video material as limitations.
estimates.moderator_quote: The DISCERN instrument measures the quality of consumer health information on treatment choices ... It employs 16 questions to evaluate the reliability and sourcing of information (Questions 1–8), specific details on information regarding treatment choices (Questions 9–15), and the overall quality rating of the material (Question 16).
estimates.notes: QUALITY per §3 (DISCERN), excluded from prevalence: a wholly accurate video scores poorly for omitting sources, uncertainty or a no-treatment option. Recorded as the share in the best-performing band because that is the verbatim share; the complement (88.5% poor) is not written, as R8 bars computed complements. Reliability for DISCERN is weak (61%, then 60% after rescoring), which is why confidence is medium.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) PEMAT-A/V shares: 55.1% of videos met overall understandability criteria and 7.8% met actionability criteria, with means of 67.6% (±16.7 in the abstract, ±16.9 in the results) and 33.8% (±36.2). These are further QUALITY measures of the same corpus; one DISCERN row already represents the quality dimension and adding three more would breach R4. An adjudicator wanting the strictest quality share should take actionability (7.8%). (2) Mean DISCERN, understandability and actionability scores and the per-question and per-item figures: scale means, not shares. (3) Clinical-criteria coverage (highest item, mention of reversal possibility, 46.2%; lowest, complications with a prior varicocele, 1.3%; none above 50%): omission measures, not falsity. (4) Source and speaker composition (hospital systems 41%, private practice 32%, other 27%; educational 69%, personal blog 18%, TV/news 10%, advertisement 3%; a medical doctor in 61 videos (78%), of whom 53 (87%) were urologists and 38 (62%) promoted their own practice): corpus attributes, not misinformation shares. (5) View, like and dislike counts (mean 216,672 views, 16,900,379 total; the single most-viewed video at 6,441,400 views scored 20, “very poor”): engagement figures, not exposure shares with a misinformation numerator. Note this paper contains no exposure denominator, so the widely-quoted reach of these videos cannot be turned into an EXPOSURE row. (6) Background prevalence figures cited from other studies (vasectomy failure 0.15%; internet use 81%/90%; knowledge rates 54% vs 96%; racial utilisation gaps): all from other publications, barred by R8. JUDGEMENT CALL: the false-statement variable has no written codebook definition beyond three illustrative categories, and its reliability is only implied by the 91% agreement figure for “study-specific characteristics” as a block, not reported for the item itself.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. Single keyword search (“vasectomy”) on 18 May 2020; the first 100 results were screened by one author, excluding duplicates, irrelevant videos and videos where vasectomy was ancillary, leaving 78. Each video was rated with the DISCERN instrument (16 items) and PEMAT-A/V (13 understandability, 4 actionability items), plus study-specific video characteristics and clinical variables derived from the AUA and CUA vasectomy guidelines and a systematic review, each scored 0/1. Coding was single-rater in practice: a medical student coded 100% of videos and supplied the analysed data, and a urology resident recoded a randomly selected 40% for reliability. Percent absolute agreement was 91% for study-specific characteristics, 85% for PEMAT-A/V and only 61% for DISCERN, so a third reviewer rescored all videos for DISCERN and agreement remained at 60%. Analysis in Excel and STATA 14. Stated limitations: results date quickly, DISCERN partial scores are subjective and its reliability was low, DISCERN was not validated for video, raters had above-population health literacy, sexual-function content was not assessed, and the study-specific clinical criteria are not themselves a validated tool. No IRB review (no human subjects); no funding; no declared conflicts.
rob.item6_quote: Clinical variables based on the American Urological Association vasectomy guidelines, Canadian Urological Association guidelines and a systematic review on the safety and effectiveness of vasectomy, were also collected ... All clinical variables were scored as no (0) or yes (1), and the total percentage meeting criteria for each item was computed.
rob.item10_quote: False statements regarding vasectomy were made in 14 (17.9%) videos.
